My name is Greg and I have been a medical provider in my community for a decade but also an active participant in the healthcare system to tell everyone that we can do better and be better than what our injuries suggest.

An active life has a cost. I’ve paid it and kept going.

Two lists, one person. The first is what I chased. The second is what it took to keep chasing it.

What I did

  • 3rd-degree Black Belt and national-level Taekwondo competitor
  • Surfing, for the love of the ocean
  • Skimboarding the waves of Santa Cruz
  • Backpacking up Heaven’s Peak, Yosemite, solo
  • Bouldering internationally
  • Golfing, for the long game
  • Physical therapist and manual therapist, working with patients exclusively with my hands, not just prescribing a list of exercises

What it cost

  • Both wrists fractured
  • Left ankle fracture
  • Severe right shoulder sprain
  • Repeated collarbone fractures, then ORIF surgery on the left
  • Years of nerve and neck pain
  • Ruptured right eardrum
  • Multiple concussions
  • Severed extensor tendon in my left toe

My story

Like many athletes, I loved my sports to the point where one day the cost was my body.

My life-changing injury wasn’t my first fracture, or my second. It was possibly my fourth fracture of the collarbone. I trusted a health professional with the repair, and I ended up with a plate in my body that would still be there today if I hadn’t been persistent. It took four orthopedic surgeons declining before the plate and screws came out.

I was told I would live with the nerve and neck pain for life, and that the numbness would eventually go away. For six years I felt like a prisoner of my own body. Only when the plate and screws were removed did I see hope for my future.

People are not broken cars to be cut open and bolted back together.

I want a future where people are treated as living beings who can heal when given the right environment. The prescription for total health starts with the organ system that supports all the others: our muscles. How I treat the body depends on building and controlling the muscular system, which relies on neurological connection and a real understanding of anatomy.

I hope my story shows that anyone can overcome a history of multiple injuries, feel young again, and participate in all that life has to offer.

Muscle and nerve first

The deep muscles of our body interrelate, building the foundation for the spine and, most important, our breathing muscles. If you aren’t aware of these connections, I hope to be the one who explains them clearly.

My goal: help people with injury histories move well again.
